summary: Tractate Yoma daf 78a covers: Temple river bubbles up from beneath the threshold and becomes mighty; Crossing water on Yom Kippur: does it constitute prohibited bathing?; Cooling without bathing: damp clay, fruit, cups, and a pre-soaked cloth; Rain water, river crossing, measuring bathing by amount; Unresolved question about water crossing and the shoe prohibition.

display.whats: Temple river bubbles up from beneath the threshold and becomes mighty
display.hint: The aggadic description of the future Temple river: it begins as a trickle from beneath the Temple threshold and grows into a mighty river that cannot be crossed on foot.
display.title: Bubbles to Sea: The Temple River's Origin

learning.ahaMoment: From under the threshold, not from above: the blessing is grounded in the foundation of the holy space itself, not in something external to it.
learning.memoryAnchor: Bubbles from beneath the threshold - holiness rises from the ground up, then grows to an uncrossable sea.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does Ezekiel's river begin as bubbles beneath the Temple threshold rather than from above?
learning.coreTension: Between the Temple's threshold as the symbolic entry point (suggesting the river should flow from above, outward) and the image of the river emerging from beneath the threshold itself.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara emphasizes the threshold as the precise origin point. The blessing comes from beneath the holy space - not just from the Temple building but from its very foundation. This grounds divine blessing in the physical structure of the sanctuary.

takeaway.text: The eschatological river's origin beneath the threshold teaches that the Temple's holiness is literally grounded - embedded in the foundation, not merely symbolic - and all future blessing flows from that physical and spiritual root.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may not register the significance of 'beneath' the threshold; the Gemara's careful attention to this detail reveals the depth of the theological claim.

argumentFlow.label: The growing spring becomes a river of purification
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The future spring strengthens past the Temple threshold until it reaches the opening of David's house, where it becomes a flowing river in which zavim, zavot, menstruating women, and women after childbirth bathe to purify, as Zechariah foretells a fountain opened for purification.

argumentFlow.label: Rejecting Rav Yosef's neck-deep mikveh requirement
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav Yosef infers from the verse that a menstruating woman must immerse in water deep enough to sit up to her neck. The Gemara rules against him: depth is irrelevant, and a ritual bath is valid as long as the water can cover an entire adult body.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners take Rav Yosef's neck-deep image as the operative law for mikveh dimensions.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara explicitly does not follow Rav Yosef. The verse's imagery is not the standard; the accepted measure is simply that the water suffice to cover a person's whole body.

visualizableElements.item: Temple river bubbles up from beneath the threshold

quizSeeds.question: Why does the Gemara reject Rav Yosef's claim that a mikveh must be deep enough to sit neck-high?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the halachic requirement is volume, not depth. A ritual bath is valid as long as it can cover an entire adult body at once; how deep one can sit in it is not the criterion.

display.whats: Crossing water on Yom Kippur: does it constitute prohibited bathing?
display.hint: The Gemara asks whether crossing a river or stream on Yom Kippur constitutes the prohibited bathing. The answer depends on intent and manner of crossing.
display.title: River Crossing on Yom Kippur

learning.ahaMoment: Purpose and intention define the act: crossing a river is travel, not bathing - the same water contact can be prohibited or permitted depending on why you are in the water.
learning.memoryAnchor: Cross to get there, not to bathe: intent determines whether water contact is prohibited.
learning.learnerQuestion: If you must cross a river on Yom Kippur, does wading through it violate the bathing prohibition?
learning.coreTension: Between the bathing prohibition (which covers contact with water) and the practical necessity of crossing a body of water for legitimate purposes.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara distinguishes purposeful bathing (prohibited) from incidental wetting while crossing for a legitimate reason (not prohibited). The prohibition targets the pleasure-act of bathing, not every form of water contact.

takeaway.text: The YK bathing prohibition targets the act of bathing as pleasure-seeking; incidental water contact incurred while doing something else for a legitimate purpose does not violate it.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may think any contact with water on YK violates the prohibition; the distinction is between purposeful bathing and incidental wetting.

argumentFlow.label: Crossing water in shoes on Shabbat
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Crossing water is straightforward on Yom Kippur because no shoes are worn, but on Shabbat shoes raise a concern: a shoe might slip off in the water and one would pick it up, violating carrying. Nechemya reports seeing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi cross a pool on Shabbat while still wearing their shoes.

argumentFlow.label: Tight shoes versus loose sandals
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Shoes can be tied tightly, so the concern is lighter, but sandals fit loosely and might come off in the water. Rav Richumi saw Ravina cross a river in sandals, yet Rav Ashi rules that one should not cross in sandals ab initio, lest one fall off and he carry it on Shabbat.

argumentFlow.label: Ravina's absence from the lecture
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Exilarch lectured in Hagronya and Ravina did not attend. The next day Rafram, to dispel any resentment, asked Ravina why he was absent, and Ravina explained that his foot hurt, specifically the back of the foot, which made wearing closed shoes difficult.

argumentFlow.label: Ravina applies Rav Ashi's sandal ruling to himself
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rafram suggested heel-exposing sandals, but Ravina noted he would have had to cross a pool. When Rafram said to cross in the sandals, Ravina invoked Rav Ashi's ruling that one should not cross water in sandals ab initio, showing his absence reflected halachic caution, not disrespect.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners assume the water-crossing rules are the same on Yom Kippur and Shabbat.
misconceptions.correction: The two days raise different concerns. On Yom Kippur no shoes are worn, so crossing is simple; on Shabbat the live issue is footwear slipping off and being carried, which is why the discussion centers on shoes versus sandals.

quizSeeds.question: Why is crossing water in sandals on Shabbat more problematic than crossing in shoes?
quizSeeds.answer: Shoes can be tied on tightly, but sandals fit loosely and may slip off in the water. If a sandal comes off and one picks it up, he violates the Shabbat prohibition of carrying, so Rav Ashi forbids crossing in sandals ab initio.

quizSeeds.question: How does Ravina's explanation for missing the lecture turn on a point of law?
quizSeeds.answer: Ravina's foot pain ruled out closed shoes, sandals would have failed crossing a pool because of Rav Ashi's ban on crossing water in sandals, so he had no permissible footwear for the trip. His absence was a halachic constraint, not a slight to the Exilarch.

display.whats: Sitting on damp clay forbidden; cooling with fruit permitted; cooling vessels (Rabba's baby, Rava's silver cup) debated by fullness and material; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's pre-soaked, wrung-out cloth; a dispute over which practice fit which fast
display.hint: What methods of cooling off on Yom Kippur avoid the bathing prohibition, and why does the Gemara dispute whether an empty cup may be used?
display.title: Cooling Without Bathing: Clay, Cups, and Cloths

learning.ahaMoment: The disputes turn on whether a method risks actual water contact with the body - which is itself the bathing prohibition - not on whether it merely feels cool: a full or leaky (ceramic) vessel spills or seeps water onto the skin and is forbidden as bathing, while fruit or a cold baby cool the body without any water touching it at all, and a cloth is governed by a separate concern (wringing) rather than by water contact.
learning.memoryAnchor: Damp clay: forbidden. Fruit: permitted. Cup: debated (empty silver - maybe; ceramic - never). Pre-wrung cloth: permitted, but only if wrung out before the fast.
learning.learnerQuestion: What methods of cooling off on Yom Kippur avoid the bathing prohibition, and why does the Gemara dispute whether an empty cup may be used?
learning.coreTension: Between wanting relief from heat on Yom Kippur and the narrower, harder-to-pin-down concerns (spilling, wringing) that actually drive each ruling, rather than a single blanket rule against coolness.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara works through a series of cooling methods and isolates what actually makes each one permitted or forbidden: damp clay is forbidden because contact itself dampens the body; fruit is permitted because it isn't water; a vessel's permissibility turns on whether it might spill (full vs. empty, silver vs. ceramic); and a cloth is permitted only if it was soaked and wrung out before the fast, since wringing itself is a separate Yom Kippur prohibition.

takeaway.text: Cooling off on Yom Kippur is not banned as such; specific methods are forbidden only when they risk actual water contact with the body - which is itself the bathing prohibition, as with a full or ceramic vessel - while methods with no water contact (fruit, a cold body) are permitted, and a cloth's permissibility turns on a separate concern: whether it was wrung out before the fast, since wringing itself is forbidden on Yom Kippur.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may look for one uniform rule about coolness on Yom Kippur; the Gemara instead evaluates each method by a different underlying risk - spilling for vessels, wringing for cloths - so superficially similar acts can land on opposite sides.

argumentFlow.label: Sitting on wet clay and cooling with fruit
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Yehuda bar Gerogarot forbids sitting on damp clay on Yom Kippur; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi limits this to clay so wet it dampens what touches it, and Abaye requires it be wet enough to wet something else. Rav Yehuda permits cooling oneself with fruit, which is not considered bathing, as he himself did with a squash.

argumentFlow.label: Cooling vessels: full versus empty, silver versus ceramic
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabba cooled himself with a cold baby, Rava with a silver cup. Rav Pappa rules a full silver cup is forbidden but an empty one permitted; a ceramic cup is forbidden either way because water seeps through. Rav Ashi adds that even an empty silver cup is forbidden, since it may slip and spill.

argumentFlow.label: The pre-soaked, wrung-out cloth of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Ze'eira bar Chama relays that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi prepared a cloth before Yom Kippur by soaking and wringing it nearly dry, then wiped his face, hands, and feet with it the next day. For the eve of the Ninth of Av, a rabbinic fast, he soaked the cloth and passed it over his eyes.

argumentFlow.label: A dispute over which practice fit which fast
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabba bar Mari reported the practice with the days reversed. Rabbi Ya'akov challenged Rabbi Yirmeya bar Tachlifa that the wringing he described for Yom Kippur was really for the Ninth of Av, since Yom Kippur carries the same wringing prohibition as Shabbat and the cloth could not be wrung that day.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners think any cooling or wiping with moisture is simply bathing and therefore banned on Yom Kippur.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara permits cooling with fruit, an empty cup, or a pre-wrung cloth, because none provides the pleasure of washing; the controlling concerns are spilling water on the body and the separate prohibition of wringing, not contact with coolness as such.

visualizableElements.item: Cooling methods on Yom Kippur: damp clay forbidden, fruit permitted, cup disputed by fullness/material, and a pre-soaked wrung-out cloth

quizSeeds.question: Why is a full silver cup forbidden for cooling on Yom Kippur while an empty one is debated?
quizSeeds.answer: A full cup risks spilling water onto the body, which approaches bathing. Rav Pappa permits an empty silver cup, but Rav Ashi forbids even that, since it may slip from the hand and spill. A ceramic cup is forbidden regardless because water seeps through its walls.

quizSeeds.question: What is the key distinction between the cloth practice for Yom Kippur and for the Ninth of Av?
quizSeeds.answer: On Yom Kippur the cloth had to be soaked and wrung out before the fast, because wringing is forbidden on Yom Kippur just as on Shabbat. The Ninth of Av, being only rabbinic, allowed greater leniency with the cloth, which is why the two practices were not interchangeable.

sugyot.finalRuling: Sitting on clay wet enough to dampen what touches it is forbidden on Yom Kippur; cooling with fruit is permitted, as is wiping with a cloth soaked and wrung out before the fast begins, since wringing itself is forbidden on Yom Kippur as on Shabbat. Cooling with a vessel is disputed: an empty cup is permitted according to Rav Pappa but forbidden according to Rav Ashi (who worries it may slip and spill), while a ceramic vessel is forbidden either way because water seeps through it.

display.whats: Rain water, river crossing, measuring bathing by amount
display.hint: Crossing rain puddles or rivers on YK raises questions about the bathing prohibition; the measurement of 'bathing' is discussed.
display.title: Puddles and Rivers: Measuring Prohibited Bathing

learning.ahaMoment: You can get wet crossing a puddle on Yom Kippur without violating the prohibition: the Talmud's analysis is about the act, not the wetness.
learning.memoryAnchor: Puddles and rivers: the question is the quality of the act (bathing vs. crossing), not the volume of water.
learning.learnerQuestion: Is there a minimum amount of water that triggers the Yom Kippur bathing prohibition?
learning.coreTension: Between a prohibition defined by the act of bathing (suggesting any water contact counts) and the practical reality that incidental wetting from puddles or shallow crossings seems qualitatively different from bathing.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara explores whether the character of the act or the quantity of water is the operative criterion. The analysis leans toward the character of the act: casual wetting incidental to movement is not the prohibited bathing.

takeaway.text: The criterion for prohibited bathing is the character of the act rather than the quantity of water; the prohibition targets intentional bathing for pleasure or comfort, not incidental wetting.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume any amount of water triggers the prohibition; recognizing that quality of act, not quantity of water, is the key criterion resolves the apparent over-breadth.

argumentFlow.label: Must a scholarly Elder get the Nasi's permission to permit firstborns?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav Menashya bar Tachalifa relays a question put to Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat: must an Elder who studies in the yeshiva obtain the Nasi's authorization to rule firstborn animals permitted by inspecting their blemishes, as others must, or is his standing sufficient on its own?

argumentFlow.label: The reason behind the permission requirement
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara explains, citing Rav Idi bar Avin, that the Nasi's authority to grant permission was instituted to honor his house. So the question is whether even a yeshiva Elder must seek it to honor the Nasi, or is exempt. Rav Tzadok testified he saw Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, a yeshiva Elder, ask the prior Nasi for such permission.

argumentFlow.label: Rabbi Abba reframes the incident as a halachic question
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Abba corrects the account: Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra was a priest, and his query was not about the Nasi's permission but a point of law, whether priests, suspected of blemishing firstborns after the Temple's destruction, are believed. The matter was resolved by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that one suspect about himself is still believed about others.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners read the firstborn-permission passage as plainly about whether scholars must defer to the Nasi.
misconceptions.correction: Rabbi Abba shows the cited precedent was really a question of priestly credibility regarding blemishes, not of seeking the Nasi's authorization, so the supposed proof about a scholar needing permission does not actually establish that.

visualizableElements.item: Rain water, river crossing, measuring bathing by a

quizSeeds.question: Why was the Nasi's authority to grant permission to rule on firstborns established?
quizSeeds.answer: To raise the stature of the Nasi's house. Because seeking his permission itself honors the Nasi, the question arises whether even a Torah scholar of standing must request it, or whether his own learning exempts him.

quizSeeds.question: How does Rabbi Abba reinterpret the testimony about Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra approaching the Nasi?
quizSeeds.answer: He says it was not a request for permission at all but a halachic question. As a priest, suspected of blemishing firstborns after the Temple's destruction, Rabbi Yosei asked whether such priests are believed, resolved by the ruling that one suspect about himself is still believed about others.

sugyot.finalRuling: Crossing rain puddles or rivers on YK raises questions about the bathing prohibition; the measurement of 'bathing' is discussed.

display.whats: Unresolved question about water crossing and the shoe prohibition
display.hint: An unresolved question (teiku) about water crossing on YK and its relationship to the shoe and bathing prohibitions.
display.title: Water Crossing and Shoes: The Unresolved Question

learning.ahaMoment: Teiku is not failure - it is the Talmud's most honest answer: we do not know, and we will not pretend otherwise.
learning.memoryAnchor: Water crossing on YK: teiku - the question stays open, practice requires stringency.
learning.learnerQuestion: What does it mean when the Talmud leaves a Yom Kippur question unresolved?
learning.coreTension: Between the need for a practical ruling (what do you do when you must cross water on YK?) and the Talmud's intellectual honesty in acknowledging it cannot fully resolve the question.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara records teiku - no resolution. This is not a failure but a principled acknowledgment of the limits of halakhic derivation. In practice, unresolved doubts in biblical prohibitions require stringency.

takeaway.text: Teiku is the Talmud's principled acknowledgment that some questions exceed what legal derivation can resolve; in practice, unresolved doubts involving biblical prohibitions default to stringency.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may feel frustrated by teiku and want a definitive ruling; recognizing teiku as intellectual honesty rather than an omission is important for understanding how the Talmud works.

argumentFlow.label: May one wear cork sandals on Yom Kippur?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The same Sages raise a further question: what is the law regarding going out in sandals made of cork on Yom Kippur, given that the affliction forbids wearing a shoe. The question of whether such sandals count as a shoe is left for the discussion that continues onto the next page.

misconceptions.misconception: Learners assume only conventional leather footwear is at issue in the shoe prohibition.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara probes borderline materials like cork precisely because the prohibition turns on whether an item functions as a comforting shoe, not on a fixed material, opening a real question about unconventional footwear.

visualizableElements.item: Unresolved question about water crossing and the s

quizSeeds.question: What is the core uncertainty in the question about cork sandals on Yom Kippur?
quizSeeds.answer: Whether a cork sandal is legally a 'shoe' for the affliction of not wearing shoes. If it counts as a shoe it is forbidden; if it is too unlike a real shoe to provide that comfort, it may be permitted. The Gemara leaves this to resolve on the next page.

sugyot.finalRuling: An unresolved question (teiku) about water crossing on YK and its relationship to the shoe and bathing prohibitions.
prerequisiteKnowledge: Understanding of Yom Kippur halachic framework

rashiTranslations.en: they further asked: what is the law of going out in a sandal of

rashiTranslations.he: שעם ביוה"כ: דבר זה. נטילת
rashiTranslations.en: cork on Yom Kippur.' 'this matter' - taking

rashiTranslations.he: הרשות: להתגדר. לשון גדולה:
rashiTranslations.en: the permission. 'lehitgader' - a term of greatness.

rashiTranslations.he: למעלה מזקנו של זה. לפני זקינו של
rashiTranslations.en: 'above the beard of this one' - means before the elder of

rashiTranslations.he: נשיא זה שבדורנו: כהנים חשודין על
rashiTranslations.en: this Nasi of our generation. 'kohanim are suspect regarding'

rashiTranslations.he: מומי הבכור להתיר את האסור ואף
rashiTranslations.en: blemishes of the firstborn, to permit what is forbidden, and even

rashiTranslations.he: להטיל בו מום לפי שהבכור בזמן הזה
rashiTranslations.en: to inflict a blemish on it, since the firstborn nowadays

rashiTranslations.he: אין לו תקנה אלא אם כן יש בו מום
rashiTranslations.en: has no remedy unless it has a blemish,

rashiTranslations.he: ועל הכהן ליטפל בו משנתנוהו לו
rashiTranslations.en: and it is upon the kohen to tend to it once it was given to him

rashiTranslations.he: לשומרו ולזונו דרבי מאיר ודרבן
rashiTranslations.en: to guard and feed it - this is the view of Rabbi Meir and Rabban

rashiTranslations.he: שמעון במסכת בכורות (דף לה.): ותו
rashiTranslations.en: Shimon, in Tractate Bekhorot (35a). 'and further'

rashiTranslations.he: קמבעיא להו. קמיה דרבי אלעזר:
rashiTranslations.en: they further asked' - before Rabbi Elazar.

rashiTranslations.he: שעם
rashiTranslations.en: Cork (continues on 78b).
